Microsoft's popular Outlook and Teams are among the services impacted by Thursday's outage [File: Dado Ruvic/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
Thousands of Microsoft users reported trouble accessing their email and connecting to work apps after a widespread outage hit Outlook and other services on Thursday.
Reports of problems with Outlook, the company’s email client, climbed to about 130,000 on the outage tracking site Downdetector shortly after 1pm Eastern Time (18:00 GMT), with some users saying emails weren’t being sent or received, while others couldn’t open their inboxes.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4IBM’s biggest division ends most US foreign worker sponsorshipslist 2 of 4Ireland fears undersea cables face growing threat from ‘malign actors’list 3 of 4India bypasses own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking techlist 4 of 4Why did Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resign, and who is Colette Kress?end of list
By just before 3pm (20:00 GMT), that figure had fallen to about 77,000.
Users also reported having trouble accessing Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams and its AI assistant Copilot, along with other Microsoft 365 services. The company said the issues could impact users in any region.
Microsoft said on X that servers were unavailable and failing automatic health checks, putting pressure on those still operating. It said it was testing a configuration change to redistribute traffic that was elevated on parts of its infrastructure and restarting affected services to bring them back online.
“We’re working to safely return them to service,” the company said.
Microsoft did not state when it expected services to be fully restored.

Cargo ships are docked at the El Palito refinery pier near Puerto Cabello, Venezuela, November 22, 2025 [File: Juan Carlos Hernandez/Reuters]By Umar FarooqPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
The United States Department of State has released a report detailing what it says the US has done with more than $12bn in revenue from Venezuelan oil and mineral resources, nearly a year after it abducted the country’s leader, Nicolas Maduro.
The disclosure is part of an effort to “promote transparency and accountability in the management of these funds”, says the 53-page report, released on Thursday.

In January, US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital of Caracas, capturing Maduro and his wife and bringing them to New York City, where they are currently facing charges related to drug trafficking and torture.
Venezuela’s then-vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, took over after Maduro’s abduction and has since made agreements with Washington that saw the US take a direct stake in profits earned from the export of oil and other mineral resources from the South American country.
Since removing Maduro from power, the Trump administration has sought to directly control who buys natural resources from Venezuela and who earns profits from those sales.
US President Donald Trump issued an executive order in January establishing special bank accounts that would hold revenue from those transactions, to be eventually distributed back to Venezuela in a controlled manner.

A legal battle is under way between Argentina and the United Kingdom, triggered by an oil project off the coast of the disputed Falkland Islands.
The Argentinian government wants to stop drilling in the area by a joint British-Israeli venture, saying it should not take place until the issue of sovereignty has been resolved.

European Political Community Summit participants pose for a photo on November 12, 2026 in Dublin, the Republic of Ireland [Peter Morrison/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and DPAPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
Leaders from more than 40 European countries have gathered in Dublin for a summit dominated by the growing number of hybrid attacks across the continent.
The biannual European Political Community (EPC), a regional group established in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, brought together heads of state and government officials on Thursday to discuss the region’s fragile security, amid a new United States-backed effort to revive talks between Russia and Ukraine to end the war.

Earlier on Thursday, more than 3,700 Italian schools received hoax bomb warnings, a day after 6,300 schools were affected by a similar widespread alert.
The Republic of Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin, known as the taoiseach, said those responsible for the attacks seek to “create confusion, sow division and weaken public confidence in our democratic systems”.

Displaced Palestinian children walk through a rain-soaked tent camp after heavy rain in Deir el-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, Saturday, November 7, 2026 [Abdel Kareem Hana/AP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and APPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
A Palestinian infant has died from the cold in a tent sheltering his displaced family in southern Gaza, his father and a doctor said, as Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on winter supplies to the war-ravaged territory.
Nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq “died from hypothermia” in Khan Younis, in the southern region of the enclave, a doctor who spoke on he condition of anonymity told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How is Gaza coping with another severe winter?list 2 of 3‘Our neighbours are gone’: Gaza survivors recount horrors of deadly floodslist 3 of 3Gaza’s infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floodsend of list
Ahmed Raqiq, the baby’s father, told AFP that Kinan died after cold temperatures hit Gaza overnight.
“I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser Hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death,” he said.
“I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in a burial shroud,” he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet.
Gaza’s Civil Defence spokesman, Mahmoud Basal, confirmed the infant’s death after exposure to extreme cold, Palestinian news network Al-Quds reported.
Winter looming

Artificial intelligence safeguards, including human controls, are at the centre of a lawsuit against the world's largest tech companies [File: Patrick Sison/AP Photo]By Hoda SherifPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
A coalition of digital safety and consumer watchdogs has filed a lawsuit against the world’s top artificial intelligence (AI) developers, requesting a court-ordered freeze on AI model training and deployments.
The civil complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court by the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI, comes on the heels of a sweeping Democratic midterm victory that many analysts note could reshape, and ultimately tighten the regulatory framework for Silicon Valley.

The suit targets five tech giants – Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX – alleging the industry leaders cannot prevent their AI creations from causing “catastrophic harm”. They are demanding the companies pause their technologies until safeguards are put in place.
The lawsuit cites documented instances of AI-driven cyberattacks and other harmful behaviours, alongside the companies’ own grave admissions that their unregulated technologies could go rogue and pose an existential threat to humanity.
